messages.subject: more than one factor variable
parts:
Hej all,
i am looking for a solution to what I think must be a fairly easy topic: the usage of more than one factor variable in the detection part of an N-mix. Using only one categorical variable (e.g. WIND) plus numerical covariates DATE and TEMPerature...
for (j in 1:nsurveys){
     C[i,j,t] ~ dbin(p[i,j,t], N[i,t]) # p[i,j,t] <----
     logit(p[i,j,t]) <- alphaw[WIND[i,j,t]] + alpha[1]*DATE[i,j,t] + alpha[2]*TEMP[i,j,t]
...everything works out fine and I obtain reasonable results for the three wind categories.
alpha[1]            -0.05   0.01    -0.07    -0.05    -0.03    FALSE 1.00 1.00  2890
alpha[2]             0.02   0.01     0.00     0.02     0.04    FALSE 0.99 1.00  3000
alphaw[1]            0.91   0.03     0.86     0.91     0.96    FALSE 1.00 1.01   813
alphaw[2]            1.08   0.03     1.02     1.08     1.14    FALSE 1.00 1.01   583
alphaw[3]            0.72   0.02     0.67     0.72     0.76    FALSE 1.00 1.01   460
deviance         20902.19 145.34 20614.14 20901.89 21183.07    FALSE 1.00 1.00  3000
However, adding another categorical variable (e.g. ground FROST [yes/no])...
logit(p[i,j,t]) <- alphaw[WIND[i,j,t]] + alphaf[FROST[i,j,t]] + alpha[1]*DATE[i,j,t] + alpha[2]*TEMP[i,j,t]
...inflates the SDs (and lowers the parameters), making the mean estimates for the categories meaningless:
alpha[1]            -0.05   0.01    -0.07    -0.05    -0.03    FALSE 1.00 1.00   664
alpha[2]             0.02   0.01     0.00     0.02     0.04     TRUE 0.96 1.00  2699
alphaw[1]            0.47   4.47    -8.35     0.48     9.38     TRUE 0.54 1.00  3000
alphaw[2]            0.65   4.47    -8.17     0.66     9.58     TRUE 0.56 1.00  3000
alphaw[3]            0.28   4.47    -8.53     0.29     9.19     TRUE 0.53 1.00  3000
alphaf[1]            0.37   4.47    -8.55     0.38     9.18     TRUE 0.54 1.00  3000
alphaf[2]            0.44   4.47    -8.44     0.43     9.27     TRUE 0.54 1.00  3000
deviance         20901.60 151.70 20595.43 20902.51 21192.73    FALSE 1.00 1.01   344
The same happens when I add another of four more categorical detection variables. In case each is the only categorical variable, all is well. I suspect that i did something wrong in model formulation but checking the books and posts I did not find any hint. Can anyone bring light into the darkness?
Thank you,
Tobias.

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: AW: more than one factor variable
parts:
Dear Tobias,

 

your model is overparameterized, i.e., you try to estimate too many parameters. This is a typical linear modeling problem: how to parameterize a model with two categorical explanatory variables (in the old times called a 2-way ANOVA). In practice, you have to set to zero some parameters, and the default when fitting such a model in R or probably about any other stats program except for SPSS is to set to zero the parameter(s) associated with the first level of a factor; this requires you have a separate intercept, too. In that case, the intercept becomes the parameter for level 1 of every factor and the other levels are expressed as a difference from that reference. Exactly as what one would do when fitting models in R with lm() or glm().

 

Best regards  -- Marc

Thank you Marc,

I understand. So it is the effect parameterization that one has to apply, as in chapter 5.6 of the AHM1. Interestingly, the first factor levels are suppressed in the WINBUGS summary of the posteriors in that chapter while they do appear in my JAGS summary. Is this a difference between the two samplers?

Kind regards,
Tobias.
